disposition: Affirmed in part, reversed in part, remanded
summary: The Town executed a tax deed on the plaintiff's property after certified notices came back undelivered, then only followed up after the fact. The court holds that once a tax deed is executed, post-deed correspondence cannot satisfy the constitutional duty to take an 'additional reasonable step' before a taking; notice of the 2016 tax lien also failed because the Town had better addresses available and didn't use them, but notice of the 2018 tax lien was adequate.

holdings.rule: Under the Fourteenth Amendment, when mailed notice of a tax sale/deed is returned unclaimed, the government must take additional reasonable steps to notify the owner before taking the property, if practicable — and those steps must come before the taking, not after.

holdings.quoted_language: the government must take additional reasonable steps to attempt to provide notice to the property owner before selling his property, if it is practicable to do so

holdings.rule: Execution of a tax deed divests the owner of title and constitutes the 'taking' for due process purposes; correspondence sent after the deed's execution does not count as an additional reasonable step.
holdings.topic: Constitutional Law > Due Process > Notice Before Taking
holdings.quoted_language: its post-deed correspondences with the plaintiff did not constitute an ‘additional reasonable step[]’

holdings.rule: Common knowledge that unpaid taxes can lead to a government taking does not excuse the government from its notice obligations before taking property.

holdings.rule: Adequacy of notice for a lesser property interest (a tax lien) requires less than notice for a full taking (a tax deed), because the lien infringes less severely on property rights.

summary: Great-grandparents who had raised their great-grandchild for most of her life sought visitation after their guardianship ended, relying not on the grandparent-visitation statute but on an asserted common-law/parens patriae right to petition for visitation. The court holds that right no longer exists — it was superseded when the legislature comprehensively rewrote the visitation statutes in 1989 and 1991 — so the petitioners lacked standing and dismissal was proper.

holdings.rule: A statute abrogates the common law even without express language to that effect if it revises the entire subject matter of a common-law cause of action and is clearly designed as a substitute for it.
holdings.topic: Statutory Interpretation > Abrogation of Common Law
holdings.quoted_language: when a statute revises the entire subject of a common law cause of action and is clearly designed as a substitute, the common law is abrogated, although no express terms to that effect are used
holdings.source_of_quote: quoting Powell v. Catholic Med. Ctr., 145 N.H. 7, 11 (2000)

holdings.rule: Absent that kind of comprehensive substitution, courts will not read a statute as abrogating the common law unless the statute clearly expresses that intent.
holdings.topic: Statutory Interpretation > Abrogation of Common Law
holdings.quoted_language: [courts] will not construe a statute . . . as abrogating the common law unless the statute clearly expresses such an intention

Ward) was superseded by RSA 458:17, VI (as amended 1991) and RSA 458:17-d, and remains superseded under their successors RSA 461-A:6, V and RSA 461-A:13; great-grandparents (as opposed to grandparents/stepparents) therefore lack standing to petition for visitation.

On a question of first impression, the court holds these were excluded 'vendor payments' because the trustee, not the petitioner, had sole discretion over distributions, so the money was never legally 'owed' to her.

disposition: Affirmed in part (evidentiary ruling and self-defense jury instruction), reversed in part (falsifying-evidence conviction vacated for insufficient evidence)
summary: Defendant, convicted of second-degree murder, falsifying evidence, and reckless conduct after shooting a truck driver who approached his car window at a red light, appeals three rulings. The court upholds admission of a recorded jail call to his mother and the self-defense jury instruction requiring reasonable necessity for deadly force, but reverses the falsifying-evidence conviction because the State's circumstantial case — built on police never finding the gun — didn't exclude the rational possibility he'd simply left it at his own apartment.

holdings.rule: Evidentiary rulings, including Rule 403 prejudice/probative-value balancing, are reviewed for unsustainable exercise of discretion — whether the ruling was clearly untenable or unreasonable to the defendant's prejudice — and the court affords considerable deference to the trial court's balancing because it is best positioned to weigh prejudicial impact.
holdings.topic: Evidence > Rule 403 Balancing (Probative Value vs. Unfair Prejudice)
holdings.quoted_language: we afford considerable deference to the trial court’s determination in balancing prejudicial impact and probative worth

holdings.rule: Evidence is unfairly prejudicial when its primary purpose or effect is to appeal to the jury's sympathies, arouse its sense of horror, provoke its instinct to punish, or otherwise cause a decision based on something other than the case's established propositions.
holdings.topic: Evidence > Rule 403 Balancing (Probative Value vs. Unfair Prejudice)
holdings.quoted_language: appeal to a jury’s sympathies, arouse its sense of horror, provoke its instinct to punish

holdings.rule: The specific contradiction doctrine lets a party introduce otherwise-inadmissible evidence only to counter a misleading advantage the opposing party created by introducing admissible evidence — admitting one piece of evidence doesn't automatically 'open the door' to unrelated inadmissible evidence.
holdings.topic: Evidence > Specific Contradiction / Opening the Door Doctrine
holdings.quoted_language: a party introduces admissible evidence that creates a misleading advantage for that party, and the opposing party is then permitted to introduce previously suppressed or otherwise inadmissible evidence to counter the misleading advantage

holdings.rule: Under RSA 627:4, II, a person using deadly force in self-defense must still reasonably believe the amount of force used was reasonably necessary under the circumstances; this judicially-read-in requirement (from Etienne) survived the legislature's 2011 removal of the duty-to-retreat requirement, and 13+ years of legislative silence since Etienne reinforces that the court's construction of the statute stands.

holdings.quoted_language: The Defendant can use the amount of force which he believed was necessary under the circumstances, as long as, at the time, there were reasonable grounds for his belief.

holdings.rule: Where an element of a crime is proven solely by circumstantial evidence, that evidence must exclude all reasonable conclusions other than guilt; evidence that police simply failed to find an item (here, a firearm) where and when they looked does not necessarily exclude an innocent explanation for its absence.

disposition: Affirmed (dismissal of two indictments with prejudice upheld)
summary: The State appeals dismissal of two indictments after failing to bring an incarcerated defendant to trial within the IAD's 180-day window. The defendant had sent his request for final disposition to the wrong Hillsborough County judicial district's superior court. The court holds RSA 606-A:2's definition of 'appropriate court' doesn't require delivery to the specific court where the charges are pending — any municipal, district, or superior court within the prosecuting officer's jurisdiction suffices — so the clock started when the defendant served the wrong-district court, and dismissal with prejudice for missing the deadline was proper.

holdings.rule: Dismissal of an indictment under the IAD presents a question of law reviewed de novo; the factual findings underlying that decision are reviewed for clear error.

holdings.rule: Under RSA 606-A:2, 'appropriate court' means any municipal, district, or superior court within the prosecuting officer's jurisdiction — it does not require delivery to the specific judicial district where the charges are pending. Courts will not add a limitation the legislature omitted, particularly where other jurisdictions' analogous statutes show the legislature knows how to write that limitation when intended.

summary: Husband appeals a fault-based divorce decree that gave his wife alimony, health insurance, and an unequal share of the marital estate, including the entire verdict from her pending discrimination lawsuit and the value of his closely-held business stock. The court affirms across the board: the unequal property division was adequately explained in writing, awarding the whole lawsuit verdict to the wife alone was sustainable given the husband's total non-involvement in it, excluding the husband's undisclosed expert over a blown discovery deadline was proper, valuing his stock using the company's own periodically-revalued redemption price (without an independent appraisal) was permissible on this record, and lifetime alimony plus open-ended health coverage were adequately supported by the wife's limited education, work history, and health.

holdings.rule: Trial courts have broad discretion over property distribution and alimony in a divorce decree; findings and rulings will stand unless lacking evidential support, tainted by legal error, or the product of an unsustainable exercise of discretion.

holdings.rule: An equal division of marital property is presumed equitable under RSA 458:16-a, II unless the trial court, after considering the statutory factors, orders otherwise and provides written reasons; reciting the statutory factors together with detailed case-specific findings satisfies the written-reasons requirement even for a substantially unequal division.

holdings.rule: A trial court is not required to divide every marital asset and may award a particular asset (such as a pending lawsuit verdict) entirely to one spouse where the record supports that the other spouse didn't participate in or contribute to obtaining it and had no personal stake in the underlying claim.

case_name: State v. Luis A. Hall (a/k/a Luis J. Wilner, Joseph Wilner)
court_below: Superior Court (Hillsborough-southern) — Hampsey, J. and Groff, J.
topics: Criminal Procedure > Confession Voluntariness / Motion to Suppress
Constitutional Law > State Constitution Provides Greater Protection Than Federal
Criminal Procedure > Mistrial Standard
Evidence > Rule 403 Balancing (Probative Value vs. Unfair Prejudice)
Evidence > Prior Bad Acts (Rule 404(b) vs. Intrinsic/Same-Episode Evidence)
summary: Defendant convicted of felonious sexual assault and providing alcohol to minors appeals denial of his motion to suppress a confession, denial of a mistrial after a witness referenced the suppression hearing, and admission of testimony that he'd asked the victim and another girl to kiss each other. The court affirms all three: the confession was voluntary under the totality of the circumstances despite officers falsely implying they had forensic evidence; the ambiguous references to the suppression hearing weren't prejudicial enough to require a mistrial; and the kissing-request testimony was properly analyzed under Rules 401/403 (not 404(b)) as part of the same episode, distinguishable from Woodard because it didn't carry that case's specific risk of juror bias against homosexuality.

holdings.rule: New Hampshire courts address a State constitutional claim first and cite federal law only to aid the analysis; a separate federal constitutional analysis is unnecessary where the State Constitution affords greater protection than the Federal Constitution in that area (as it does for confession voluntariness).
holdings.topic: Constitutional Law > State Constitution Provides Greater Protection Than Federal
holdings.quoted_language: We need not conduct a separate federal constitutional analysis because our State Constitution affords the defendant greater protection than does the Federal Constitution in this area.

holdings.rule: Voluntariness of a confession is a factual question for the trial court, reviewed for whether its finding is contrary to the manifest weight of the evidence viewed most favorably to the State; the State must prove voluntariness beyond a reasonable doubt by examining the totality of the circumstances — the accused's characteristics and the details of the interrogation — to determine whether the defendant's will was overborne.
holdings.topic: Criminal Procedure > Confession Voluntariness / Motion to Suppress
holdings.quoted_language: To be considered voluntary, a confession must be the product of an essentially free and unconstrained choice and not extracted by threats, violence, direct or implied promises of any sort, or by the exertion of any improper influence.

holdings.rule: Police deception about the existence of incriminating evidence (e.g., falsely suggesting forensic evidence exists) does not by itself render a subsequent confession involuntary, so long as the deception isn't severe enough to overbear the defendant's will.
holdings.topic: Criminal Procedure > Confession Voluntariness / Motion to Suppress
holdings.source_of_quote: citing United States v. Palmer, 203 F.3d 55, 62 (1st Cir. 2000)

holdings.rule: A mistrial is warranted only where the challenged conduct is more than merely inadmissible and constitutes an irreparable injustice that jury instructions cannot cure; the trial court's denial is reviewed for unsustainable exercise of discretion, and ambiguous testimony that doesn't substantially prejudice the defendant does not require a mistrial.
holdings.topic: Criminal Procedure > Mistrial Standard
holdings.quoted_language: To justify a mistrial, the conduct must be more than merely inadmissible; it must constitute an irreparable injustice that cannot be cured by jury instructions.

holdings.rule: Evidence of conduct that is part of the same episode as the charged crime, rather than a separate 'prior bad act,' is analyzed under Rules 401 and 403 rather than Rule 404(b), and is admissible if its probative value (e.g., on intent or plan) is not substantially outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice.

holdings.quoted_language: part and parcel of the same episode

holdings.rule: Evidence implicating a defendant's same-sex conduct carries a heightened, case-specific risk of unfair prejudice from potential juror bias against homosexuality; that heightened concern from Woodard doesn't extend to evidence that doesn't involve homosexual conduct or a same-sex-assault charge.

discretion_calls.key_facts: Defendant's trial theory was that the victim initiated contact while he was asleep and he wasn't aware; the kissing-request evidence undercut that passive-recipient narrative and showed active intent toward sexual contact; unlike Woodard, it didn't involve homosexual conduct or carry that specific juror-bias risk.

topics: Property Law > Landlord-Tenant > Quiet Enjoyment / Unauthorized Entry
Statutory Interpretation > Definition of 'Willful'/'Willfully'
Civil Procedure > Preservation of Issues for Appeal > Waiver (Notice of Appeal + Briefing)
summary: Tenants sued their landlord under RSA chapter 540-A after he let carpet installers into their leased home without authorization. The trial court found the entry violated the tenants' right to quiet enjoyment but wasn't a 'willful' violation of RSA 540-A:2 because the landlord honestly (if mistakenly) believed he had consent. The court affirms, holding that 'willful' under this statute excludes acts done under a mistaken belief of the facts, consistent with how the court has read 'willful' in analogous wage and consumer-protection statutes.

holdings.rule: 'Willful' is a word of many meanings depending on the statutory context in which it's used, but New Hampshire courts have consistently interpreted it to exclude an act committed under a mistaken belief of the operative facts — a willful act is a voluntary act committed with intent to cause its result, not an accident or an act based on a mistake of fact.
holdings.topic: Statutory Interpretation > Definition of 'Willful'/'Willfully'
holdings.quoted_language: A willful act is a voluntary act committed with an intent to cause its results. It is not, by contrast, an accident or an act committed on the basis of a mistake of fact.
holdings.source_of_quote: quoting Ives v. Manchester Subaru, Inc., 126 N.H. 796, 801 (1985)

holdings.rule: RSA 540-A:2's prohibition on 'willfully' violating a tenant's rights does not impose liability on a landlord who enters the premises under an honestly mistaken understanding that the tenant had consented, even though the entry itself still violates the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.
holdings.topic: Property Law > Landlord-Tenant > Quiet Enjoyment / Unauthorized Entry

holdings.rule: An argument is waived on appeal if it was neither raised in the notice of appeal nor briefed — either failure independently forfeits the argument.

core definition of a 'willful act'; held that a wage-payment statute's willfulness requirement doesn't impose liability where the employer had a bona fide belief it wasn't obligated to pay
cites.quoted_language: was not intended to impose liability where the employer’s refusal to pay wages is based upon bona fide belief that he is not obligated to pay them

note: Not a classic negligence/premises-liability tort — this is a landlord-tenant statutory claim (quiet enjoyment/unauthorized entry under RSA ch. 540-A), closer to a quasi-tort/consumer-protection hybrid than the tort case type (negligence, premises liability, medical malpractice) still missing from the sample. Still valuable: the 'willful' definition it applies traces through wage-payment law (Ives), administrative appeals (Morgan), and older common-law cases (Hynes, Berke) — another example, like the Lambert discretion standard, of a single interpretive rule recurring across unrelated statutory schemes over decades.

case_name: Beckles & a. v. Madden, M.D. & a.
topics: Torts > Medical Malpractice > Proximate Cause
Torts > Negligence > Proximate Cause (Cause-in-Fact & Legal Cause)
Civil Procedure > Standard of Review > Summary Judgment (De Novo)
Evidence > Expert Testimony > Medical Causation Opinions
summary: Plaintiffs sued several doctors for medical malpractice, alleging their failure to diagnose a vitamin B-12 deficiency and take fall-prevention precautions caused Mr. Beckles to fall, fracture his ankle, and (through a chain of subsequent treatment) suffer a brain hemorrhage leaving him permanently disabled. The trial court granted summary judgment to the defendants, ruling the plaintiffs' medical experts gave only speculative, conclusory opinions on causation. The court reverses: viewed in the light most favorable to the plaintiffs, the experts' testimony that proper precautionary care would more likely than not have prevented the fall was sufficient to create a jury question on causation, even though some of the underlying factual assumptions (timing of appointments, patient compliance, spousal supervision) remained genuinely disputed.

holdings.rule: In a medical malpractice action under RSA 507-E:2, the plaintiff must prove by expert testimony (1) the standard of reasonable professional practice, (2) that the provider failed to meet it, and (3) that this proximately caused injuries that would not otherwise have occurred.
holdings.topic: Torts > Medical Malpractice > Proximate Cause

holdings.rule: Proximate cause has two components — cause-in-fact (the injury would not have occurred without the conduct) and legal cause (the conduct was a substantial factor in bringing about the harm, though it need not be the sole cause); the evidence must be sufficient to warrant a reasonable juror's conclusion that the causal link probably existed, meaning reasonable probability rather than mathematical certainty.
holdings.topic: Torts > Negligence > Proximate Cause (Cause-in-Fact & Legal Cause)
holdings.quoted_language: with reasonable probability, not mathematical certainty, that but for the defendant’s negligence, the harm would not have occurred
holdings.source_of_quote: quoting Bronson v. The Hitchcock Clinic, 140 N.H. 798, 802-03 (1996)

holdings.rule: Expert testimony is required to establish proximate cause in medical malpractice cases to keep the jury from engaging in idle speculation; a medical expert's competent opinion that the defendant's negligence 'probably caused' the harm supplies the necessary quantum of expert evidence, and experts need not use the statute's exact words or phrases.
holdings.topic: Evidence > Expert Testimony > Medical Causation Opinions
holdings.quoted_language: A medical expert’s competent opinion that the defendant’s negligence ‘probably caused’ the harm establishes the quantum of expert testimony necessary.

holdings.rule: A trial court's assessment of the sufficiency of expert medical testimony on summary judgment is reviewed de novo — not for clear error or unsustainable exercise of discretion — with the appellate court independently reviewing the record in the light most favorable to the non-moving party.
holdings.topic: Civil Procedure > Standard of Review > Summary Judgment (De Novo)
holdings.source_of_quote: citing Smith v. HCA Health Servs. of N.H., 159 N.H. 158, 160 (2009); rejecting defendant's argument for a deferential standard

holdings.rule: Factual assumptions underlying an expert's causation opinion — such as whether the patient would have complied with treatment or a family member would have supervised him — are questions of fact for the jury, and can be established through lay testimony rather than expert testimony; summary judgment should not be used to foreclose a plaintiff from presenting evidence on those underlying facts.
holdings.topic: Torts > Medical Malpractice > Proximate Cause

holdings.rule: Experts may permissibly opine on hypothetical circumstances so long as the facts assumed in the hypothetical are supported by evidence and resemble the case actually before the jury.
holdings.topic: Evidence > Expert Testimony > Medical Causation Opinions
holdings.source_of_quote: citing Canney v. Travelers Insurance Co., 110 N.H. 304, 305 (1970)

note: This is the first genuine negligence-family tort in the sample (medical malpractice), closing the practice-area gap flagged after Rood. It also reinforces the de novo summary-judgment standard already seen in Manutsom — here the court explicitly rejects a party's attempt to import a more deferential standard, which is itself a useful data point for a 'standard of review' topic brief.
